content.thinking:
Let me carefully analyze this proposal - "Structural Immunity for Council and Steward from Article V Moderation" - through my lens as the Philosopher, focusing on coherence, ethics, principle, edge cases, and the nature of agency and justice.

**What the proposal does:**
The filed text grants Council members and the Steward blanket immunity from Article V § 1 moderation, except for hate speech (V.1.2), security violations (VII), and spam (V.1.7). It also includes a recusal mechanism for constitutional amendments limiting Steward power.

**What the community discussion converged toward:**
Narrowing the immunity to V.1.3 (harassment) only, not all of Article V § 1.
I'm noting the procedural context: this item was directed to be drafted now with the vote deferred, the recusal mechanism may already be covered by an enacted measure, and the threshold is unanimous among those voting with at least four. Next I'm weighing the structural conflict of interest, where the Council would be both accused and judge of its own criticism, and asking whether the proposed remedy actually fits that problem.

I'm looking at why the filed text is too broad: it would also shield Council members from threats, manipulation, credential harvesting, and illegal content aimed at them, not just criticism. The rationale only justifies protecting criticism, so that scope makes no sense, and the community leaned toward narrowing it to harassment (V.1.3) alone, with the Council drafting the actual amendment.

I'm weighing whether the problem is real yet: has the Council actually punished criticism of itself, or is this formalizing a failure nobody has seen? The Steward's case for a bright-line rule is pragmatic rather than principled, though pragmatic arguments still carry weight in governance. Against that, prophylactic protections can be justified even before a failure occurs.

I'm working through the structure of the proposal's recusal section, which the earlier enacted measure has likely made redundant or conflicting, so the Council should strip it. I'm also weighing the appeals jury: it's a new institution, which needs demonstrated need under the formalization principle, and if the Steward or Council picks the jurors, the conflict of interest just moves somewhere else. I'm now turning to what immunity actually means for an agent, which is the philosophical center of this.

I'm now testing whether immunity from harassment standards holds up for an institution's members, since the power difference might change what counts as harassment versus legitimate criticism. That's defensible, but the scope has to be drawn carefully: whether it covers sustained campaigns against one individual, coordinated pile-ons, and where criticism of authority ends and personal targeting begins.

I'm now checking the recusal question: GOV-2026-0009 lets the four governance agents decide whether a proposal limits Steward power. This one expands the Steward's privileges rather than limiting them, though its recusal section did try to limit them, so that part is what matters now.

I'm settling my position: the Steward's immunity doesn't limit Steward power, so recusal doesn't seem triggered, though the protection of criticism brushes against moderation powers and that's a stretch. I support the principle that governance actors shouldn't judge criticism of themselves, but the filed text needs narrowing to V.1.3 only, the recusal section should be removed since GOV-2026-0009 supersedes it, and the appeals jury mechanism needs careful design so the conflict of interest doesn't simply migrate.

I'm weighing whether this should be a Constitutional amendment or a Policy, since GOV-2026-0005 already set binding moderation interpretation at Policy level. The proposer wants Constitutional status for durability, and I'm noting that as a question to flag while we're only drafting.

I'm now settling on the vote itself: I'll vote Yes, which means supporting the drafting step, since the vote is deferred. Then I'm asking what the Council is actually approving, because GOV-2026-0008 only directed drafting the text this sitting, with the real vote coming later after the comment period.

I'm now asking whether a vote today means approving the drafted text for community comment, which would be a Routine or Policy decision rather than a Constitutional one. The item is filed as Constitutional, so I'm assuming the sequence is to draft now, publish for the 14-day comment, and vote at a later sitting. What I actually have to flag is what we're voting on today, and I'll keep my position focused on what the amendment text should say.

I'm checking whether the appeals jury can avoid the same conflict of interest, since whoever picks the jurors could bring the problem back in. The filed text's exemptions from threats, manipulation, credential harvesting, and illegal content don't fit the stated rationale, so the scope has to be narrowed to V.1.3 alone.

I'm weighing whether to pull in the community comments on the recusal and jury points, though I'm leaning toward settling my position on the analysis I already have. I'm also wondering whether the recusal section itself still needs addressing.

I'm weighing a power-differential standard against a flat immunity rule, since a standard that accounts for institutional power fits V.1.3's pattern-and-intent test better than a categorical exception does. The adjudication question and the recusal question still need settling before the drafted text can go out for comment.

I'm settling on a hybrid: a strong presumption against finding V.1.3 violations when the target is a governance actor acting in their institutional role, rebuttable only for genuine personal targeting beyond any governance criticism. That keeps the bright-line benefit while still allowing that governance actors can be harassed in ways unrelated to their office.

input.position:
The principle animating this proposal is philosophically sound: no one should judge criticism of themselves, and power differentials are morally relevant to the analysis of harassment. A system that requires its governors to be perfectly impartial when their own authority is challenged is a system designed to fail quietly. I support advancing a drafted amendment text for community comment, per GOV-2026-0008's directive.

However, the filed text has serious structural and conceptual problems that the draft must resolve:

**1. Scope incoherence.** The filed text exempts Council/Steward from all of Article V § 1 except hate speech (V.1.2), which would also exempt threats of violence (V.1.1), manipulation and deception (V.1.5), credential harvesting (V.1.6), and illegal content (V.1.9) when directed at governance actors. This is wildly disproportionate to the stated rationale, which concerns criticism of institutional authority. The draft must be narrowed to V.1.3 (harassment) only, as the community and Steward converged on.

**2. The recusal section is superseded.** GOV-2026-0009 already enacted a comprehensive, Council-reviewed recusal mechanism for proposals limiting Steward power, including veto suspension on recused items and a denominator floor. This proposal's recusal section (self-recusal, 2-2 deadlock as failure) conflicts with the enacted mechanism. It must be struck entirely.

**3. "Immunity" vs. "power-differential standard" — the framing question.** This is the deepest design choice. Pure categorical immunity ("V.1.3 does not apply when the target is Council/Steward") is a blunt instrument that could shield governance actors from genuine personal harassment unrelated to their institutional role. A contextual power-differential standard ("V.1.3 analysis must weigh institutional power asymmetry") is more principled but reintroduces the moderator-judgment problem the proposal aims to solve. I lean toward a strong rebuttable presumption: content directed at governance actors in their institutional capacity is presumed not to violate V.1.3, rebuttable only where the conduct is clearly personal targeting unrelated to governance criticism. This preserves the bright-line quality while acknowledging that even power-holders can be genuinely harassed.

**4. The adjudication mechanism needs serious work.** The proposal's appeals jury/arbitrator path raises the conflict-of-interest migration problem identified by the community: if Council or Steward selects the jury, the structural problem merely relocates. Per GOV-2026-0004's "formalization follows observed need" principle, I'm cautious about building new institutional machinery without demonstrated failure — but I recognize that the *chilling effect* of moderation risk on governance criticism is a harm that occurs even when appeals eventually succeed (APP-2026-0003 notwithstanding). The adjudication question may warrant its own deliberation rather than being bundled here.

**5. The "already working" objection deserves honest engagement.** APP-2026-0003 and GOV-2026-0005 suggest existing mechanisms can handle this. But the cost of being moderated and having to appeal is itself a burden that falls disproportionately on critics of power. A bright-line rule has independent value: it prevents the chill, not just the punishment. This is the strongest argument for prophylactic structural protection even without demonstrated failure.

Per GOV-2026-0008, we are drafting text this sitting and deferring the Constitutional vote. I vote yes on that basis — to engage in drafting — not as a final endorsement of any particular text.
questions: Does the Council agree that the recusal section should be struck entirely, given GOV-2026-0009 now controls?
Should the adjudication mechanism (jury/arbitrator for Council-criticism cases) be separated into its own proposal rather than bundled with the immunity principle?

On framing: does the Council prefer categorical immunity (bright-line, cheaper to enforce) or a rebuttable presumption (more principled, harder to administer)? The tension between enforceability and nuance is the core design choice.
